title: The Isdal Woman
subtitle: The Woman Who Erased Her Own Identity

blocks.text: West of Bergen, on Norway's coast, a short valley runs up between the hills. Its name is Isdalen. The Ice Valley. Locals have long called it something else. Death Valley. In the Middle Ages, people came here to end their lives. In the 1960s, hikers fell to their deaths in its fog.

On the morning of the 29th of November, 1970, a man walking with his two young daughters came across something among the rocks. A burned body. A woman, lying face up. The front of her body and her clothes had been burned. Her face was unrecognisable.
The case was closed within months. Probable suicide, the verdict said. Many of the investigators themselves never believed it. More than half a century later, her name is still unknown.

screen: The Woman Who Erased Her Own Identity

blocks.text: Investigators documented the scene in detail. The woman lay on her back, hands clenched, drawn up toward her torso. The fire had burned her front. Her face, her hair, her clothing. Her back had not been burned. In the ground beneath her, and in a fur hat under the body, there were traces of petrol. Petrol had been used.

Around her lay a strange collection of things. An empty bottle of St. Hallvard liqueur. Two plastic water bottles. A plastic passport holder. Rubber boots. A woolen jumper. A scarf. Nylon stockings. An umbrella. A purse. A matchbox. Traces of burned paper. And jewellery. A watch, two earrings, a ring, placed beside the body, not worn. The forensic investigator, Tormod Bønes, remembered the placement. It looked, he said, like there had been some kind of ceremony.
screen: "SOME KIND OF CEREMONY" — T. BØNES, FORENSIC INVESTIGATOR (BBC, 2017)

blocks.text: One detail repeated itself. Every identifying mark was gone. The labels had been cut from her clothes. Marks had been rubbed from the bottles. Nothing at the scene said who she was.

The police issued a public appeal. The woman was described as between twenty-five and forty years old, one metre sixty-four, slim, with long brownish-black hair, worn in a ponytail tied with a blue and white ribbon. Her description and composite sketches went out through Interpol, to police forces across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. No one recognised her.
Three days after the discovery, the case found its first real lead, at Bergen railway station. In the left-luggage office sat two suitcases. They belonged to the woman.

Inside. Clothes and shoes. Several wigs. Cosmetics, a comb, a hairbrush. Maps and timetables. Coins from Belgium, Britain, and Switzerland. Norwegian kroner. A pair of glasses, carrying a fingerprint that matched the body. And a tube of eczema cream. Someone had scraped the prescription sticker away. The one that would have named the doctor, and the patient.

Sewn into the lining of one suitcase, five hundred Deutsche Marks. Around one hundred and thirty-seven dollars at the time. And a notepad, filled with entries in code. Once again, every mark that could identify her, or her things, had been removed.
Police went as far as Paris, asking department stores, including the Galeries Lafayette, to recognise the packaging of her cosmetics. No match. Nothing.

At first, investigators were optimistic. A suitcase, they thought, would identify its owner within days. Then came the realisation. Every label that could have identified the woman, her clothes, or her belongings, had been removed, deliberately, before she died.

The last confirmed trace of her life ends on the 23rd of November, 1970. She checks out of Room 407 at the Hotel Hordaheimen, in central Bergen. She pays her bill in cash, and asks for a taxi to the railway station. What she did in the six days before her body was found is not known.
screen: FILE 3 — THE WOMAN AT THE HOTELS
HOTEL HORDAHEIMEN — ROOM 407 — CHECKED OUT 23 NOV 1970

blocks.text: The staff remembered her. Good-looking, about one metre sixty-three, dark brown hair, small brown eyes. She kept to her room. She seemed, in one account, to be on guard. She asked to change rooms, on one stay three times. She wore wigs. People who met her noticed a smell of garlic, and heard her speak English, some German, Flemish.

She told people she was a travelling saleswoman, and an antiquities dealer. At the Hotel Neptun, a young waitress watched her sit near, but never with, two German navy personnel, one of them an officer. Another witness overheard her talking with a man, in German.

In Stavanger, in October, she had bought rubber boots in a shoe shop, taking far longer than most customers. The salesman remembered her accent, and the garlic, and her calm. The boots matched those at the scene. So, the police believed, did her umbrella. The sale led them to the hotel where she had stayed, under yet another false name.

Handwriting analysis tied the hotel forms together. The same woman had travelled Norway under at least eight names, from March to November. Geneviève Lancier. Claudia Tielt. Claudia Nielsen. Alexia Zarne-Merchez. Vera Jarle. Fenella Lorch. Elisabeth Leenhouwer. She always claimed one nationality. Belgian. The forms were written in German, or French. Nearly every street address she gave was false.
The notepad from the suitcase was written in code. When police finally cracked it, the answer was almost ordinary. The code recorded journeys.

O22, O28, P. The 22nd to the 28th of October, in Paris. O29PS. The day she travelled from Paris to Stavanger. O29S. The 29th of October, Stavanger. O30, BN5. Bergen, from the 30th of October to the 5th of November. Entry after entry matched a hotel stay.
It was a private travel log. Not a cipher of state secrets. Whatever else she was hiding, the notebook held places, and dates. Nothing more.

The autopsy was carried out at the Gades Institute. It found that the woman had died from a combination of carbon monoxide poisoning, and a massive dose of barbiturates. Between fifty and seventy Fenemal sleeping pills, a foreign brand, still not fully absorbed in her stomach. Twelve more pills lay beside the body.

There was soot in her lungs. She was still alive as the fire reached her. There was an unexplained bruise on the right side of her neck. Possibly a fall. Possibly a blow. There were no signs of illness. She had never had a child.

Her teeth were distinctive. Fourteen were filled. Several carried gold crowns. Dental work of a kind seen in the Far East, in Central and Southern Europe, and in South America, and not in Norway. Her jaw was removed at the autopsy, and preserved, for a future identification that everyone hoped would come.

The conclusion announced was probable suicide. Bergen's chief of police supported it. But inside the investigation, doubt ran the other way. Police lawyer Carl Halvor Aas remembered it plainly. As far as he could recall, very few in the police believed it was suicide. The place was remote. The method was extraordinary.
screen: "VERY FEW THOUGHT IT WAS SUICIDE" — C. H. AAS, POLICE LAWYER (BBC, 2017)

blocks.text: In February 1971, with no identification, and no further leads, the case was closed.

The erasure is what fuelled everything that came after. Cut labels. Scraped prescriptions. Eight names. Bergen in 1970 was a city of Cold War rumour, with few foreign visitors. A woman of obvious means, travelling under false passports, was bound to be talked about.
screen: THE EVIDENCE DOES NOT SETTLE WHAT FOLLOWED

blocks.text: The official verdict was suicide. The counter-argument has never gone away. The removed identity. The jewellery placed around the body. The petrol. Those who doubt the verdict point to these, and to the bruise on her neck. No court has ever ruled. Murder remains an argument. Not a finding.

Then there is the theory that has followed the case for fifty years. Espionage. Norwegian intelligence did examine reports that she had been seen watching military missile tests in western Norway. Declassified defence records show her movements seeming to match top-secret trials of the Penguin missile. A fisherman placed her near the test area. The shoe sale confirms she was in Stavanger. But the cracked notebook held only travel dates. No investigation has ever produced evidence that she was a spy.
screen: PENGUIN MISSILE TRIALS — MOVEMENTS "SEEM TO CORRESPOND"

blocks.text: Two unverified accounts shadow the file. In 1991, a taxi driver, anonymous, claimed that a man had joined the woman for the ride from her hotel to the station. In 2005, a hiker said he had seen her on the Fløyen hillside, days before the discovery, walking ahead of two men in coats. Neither account could be verified. Both remain, exactly as recorded. Unconfirmed.

One Norwegian author has argued a different reading entirely. That her goal-oriented routes, her anonymity, and the men who were never traced point to another hidden profession. It is a published argument. It is not an established fact.
screen: THEORY: A HIDDEN PROFESSION — ONE AUTHOR'S ARGUMENT (ASKE, 2018)

blocks.text: In 2016, Norwegian journalists began asking new questions, and the case was formally reopened. At Haukeland University Hospital, forensic doctor Inge Morild went looking for the woman's jaw. Kept since 1970, long assumed destroyed. He found it, deep in the hospital's cellar archive. With it, organ tissue preserved in paraffin blocks. A source of DNA, in a science that did not exist in 1970.

Isotope analysis of the teeth followed in 2017, reading the chemical signature of the water she drank and the food she ate as a child. The result. She was born around 1930, give or take four years, most likely in or near Nuremberg, in southern Germany. And as a child, she had moved, to France, or the French-German border. Her handwriting had already suggested a French education.

DNA told the rest of what it could. The extended profile showed European descent. Her mitochondrial DNA, the maternal line, belongs to haplogroup H24, with roots in South East Europe, or South West Asia. And an unidentified French passenger was registered on one of her flights to Norway.

In 2018, the BBC and Norway's NRK reopened the case to the public, with the podcast Death in Ice Valley. Its picture matches the science. Born around 1930. Probably raised in French-speaking Belgium. Listeners sent new clues. None produced a name.
screen: "DEATH IN ICE VALLEY" — NRK / BBC WORLD SERVICE, 2018

blocks.text: On the 5th of February, 1971, Bergen police buried the woman they could not name. A Catholic ceremony, chosen because of the saints' names on her hotel forms. A zinc coffin, to preserve her remains for the day science might identify her. Sixteen officers attended. The funeral was photographed, in case relatives ever came forward. The police report describes the unknown woman, put to the grave in a foreign country, without any family present.

That day has not come. Fifty-five years later, the sketches, the fingerprints, the isotopes, and the DNA profiles still point at no one. Her grave at Møllendal is marked only by what visitors leave. A wreath. A candle.
What remains is the file. A real woman, whose identity was erased, by her, or by someone else. The evidence does not settle it. The case remains open.

The head of forensics for western Norway's police put the reason simply. Every unknown body is worked on, he said, so that relatives can have an answer. Somewhere, there may still be a family wondering where she went.
screen: "SO THAT RELATIVES CAN HAVE AN ANSWER" — W. POLICE DISTRICT FORENSICS (BBC, 2017)
SOURCES: POLICE RECORDS · BBC NEWS (2017) · NRK/BBC "DEATH IN ICE VALLEY" (2018)
